issues.legal_issue: A nationalisation amendment that terminates coal-mining leases and permits later prospecting and leasing is within Parliament’s legislative competence when it advances the conservation, regulation and planned development of coal resources.
material_facts: The amendment barred most persons from carrying on coal-mining operations and terminated most existing coal-mining leases and sub-leases.

It permitted the Central Government and specified public entities to obtain prospecting licences or mining leases over the affected land, allowing investigation and planned development before mining resumed.
The wider statutory scheme imposed a duty to take steps for the conservation and development of minerals.
The petitioners argued that the amendment lacked an obligation to work the mines and therefore amounted to prohibition rather than regulation or development.
issues.conclusion: Parliament had legislative competence to enact the amendment; its provisions furthered the public-interest purpose of regulating mines and developing mineral resources through conservation, investigation and planned exploitation.
issues.legal_principle: The legislative power over regulation of mines and mineral development, when placed under Union control in the public interest, is purposive, but regulation includes conservation and may involve restricting or temporarily preventing unplanned working. Whether the chosen means achieve the legislative purpose is principally a matter of legislative policy. An enabling expression may carry a duty to act with reasonable promptitude when the nature and object of the power require it. The Court relied on Entry 54 of List I and the statutory duty of mineral conservation and development in Section 18 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957; it also considered K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Attorney-General for Ontario v. Attorney-General for Canada, Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, and Julius v. Bishop of Oxford.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A person brings a constitutional writ challenge to the legislative authority for a measure affecting mining rights or operations.
predicates.measure_targets_unplanned_mining: The measure restricts existing mining rights or operations to address unplanned or unscientific extraction.
predicates.measure_enables_later_planned_exploratio: The measure allows public authorities or designated public entities to investigate, prospect or obtain mining rights for planned future development.
predicates.public_resource_conservation_is_part_of_: The surrounding legal scheme requires or pursues conservation and development of the mineral resource.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenge concerns a measure that restricts unplanned mining while enabling later planned exploration within a resource-conservation scheme, the legislature has competence to enact it.

issues.legal_issue: A composite lease for coal and fireclay does not permit fireclay extraction where that extraction necessarily involves coal mining, even though the composite mine falls outside the statutory definition of a coal mine.
material_facts: A petitioner held a single lease covering both coal and fireclay in a mine with alternating seams of the two minerals.
The petitioner stated that the minerals were so intermingled that fireclay could not be mined without disturbing or mining coal.
The amendment prohibited persons outside specified categories from conducting coal-mining operations and provided penal consequences for unauthorised coal mining.

The Court permitted the composite lessees to mine fireclay only so far as they did not conduct coal-mining operations, but concluded that the lessees’ own account made such separate extraction impossible.
issues.conclusion: A composite mine containing coal and fireclay was outside the statutory definition of a coal mine, but a lessee could mine fireclay only if doing so involved no coal-mining operation; where fireclay extraction necessarily involved coal mining, the lessee could not mine the fireclay and risked prosecution.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of a coal mine in Section 2(b) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, read against the differently worded definition of a coking coal mine in Section 3(c) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, did not include a composite coal-and-fireclay mine. But the prohibition on unauthorised coal-mining operations in Section 3(3)(a), and the penalty in Section 30(2) of the 1973 Act, applied regardless of whether the lease was composite. A lessee could therefore extract fireclay only without conducting a coal-mining operation.

rule.if: challenge_to_mining_restrictions and composite_mining_lease and coal_and_fireclay_are_interleaved and fireclay_extraction_requires_coal_mining

predicates.challenge_to_mining_restrictions: A lessee challenges restrictions on mining under a statutory regime governing coal operations.
predicates.composite_mining_lease: The lessee holds one lease covering coal and another mineral.
predicates.coal_and_fireclay_are_interleaved: The coal and fireclay occur in alternating or otherwise intermingled deposits.
predicates.fireclay_extraction_requires_coal_mining: Extracting the fireclay necessarily entails conducting a coal-mining operation.

issues.definition: If a lessee challenges mining restrictions under a coal regime, holds a composite lease over intermingled coal and fireclay, and cannot extract the fireclay without coal mining, the lessee cannot extract the fireclay without authority to mine coal.

issues.legal_issue: Terminating surviving coal-mining leases extinguishes the lessees’ residual rights rather than acquiring those rights for the State, and does not unlawfully discriminate against lessees whose identifiable interests were acquired under earlier nationalisation measures.
material_facts: Earlier measures took over management of coal mines and nationalised scheduled mines, providing amounts for the interests acquired.
The amendment terminated leases and sub-leases that remained outstanding after those measures, including interests the Court described as precarious or not readily identifiable.
The amendment did not itself transfer the terminated leasehold interests to the State; a public entity had to take a further positive step to obtain a new prospecting licence or mining lease.
The amendment formed part of a scheme intended to reorganise coal mining and promote its rational, coordinated and scientific development.
The petitioners argued that termination without payment was an acquisition and discriminated against lessees who had received payment under earlier measures.
issues.conclusion: The amendment extinguished the residual leasehold rights rather than acquiring them for the State; the affected lessees were differently situated from owners whose identifiable interests had been acquired and paid for, so the termination did not violate Article 14 or amount to an uncompensated acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(e), as applicable at the relevant time, protected laws providing for extinguishment or modification of mineral-related rights from invalidity under Articles 14, 19 and 31. Under Article 31(2A), deprivation is not treated as compulsory acquisition where the law does not provide for transfer of ownership or the right to possession to the State or a State-controlled corporation. Extinguishment and acquisition are distinct where the State is not the beneficiary of the terminated rights. The Court relied on Article 31A(1)(e) and Article 31(2A), and distinguished Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab and Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India; it also applied the substance-over-form approach discussed in Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A holder brings a constitutional writ challenge to legislation terminating a mining interest.
predicates.surviving_mining_rights_are_terminated: The legislation terminates mining rights that remained outstanding after earlier management or nationalisation measures.
predicates.terminated_rights_do_not_vest_in_the_sta: The legislation does not itself transfer the terminated rights to the State or a State-controlled entity, and a further step is required to obtain new rights.
predicates.earlier_compensated_interests_were_more_: Earlier measures acquired identifiable mining interests and provided payment for those interests, unlike the residual interests later terminated.

issues.definition: When legislation terminates surviving mining rights without vesting them in the State, and earlier compensated interests were more identifiable, the termination is treated as extinguishment rather than State acquisition and as non-discriminatory.
